case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Colorado may apply its public-accommodations law to compel a website designer to create custom wedding websites celebrating same-sex marriages (and to restrict what she may say about that service), consistent with the First Amendment.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. amend. I (Free Speech Clause, and related compelled-speech doctrine; Free Exercise issues appear in the background) as applied to Colorado Anti-Discrimination Act (CADA) public-accommodations provisions and the CADA/CCRC 'Communication Clause' regulating discriminatory statements/advertising.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (303 Creative LLC and Lorie Smith) argue that creating custom wedding websites is inherently expressive activity, so forcing them to design sites celebrating same-sex weddings compels speech and viewpoint endorsement in violation of the Free Speech Clause; they also challenge Colorado’s related restrictions on announcing their religious-based limitation on services (the 'Communication Clause') as unconstitutional speech regulation. They frame the case as part of a broader pattern of enforcing public-accommodations laws against religiously motivated businesses and contend that Supreme Court review is needed because Masterpiece Cakeshop did not resolve the merits and left uncertainty and a patchwork of protections.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents (Colorado officials charged with enforcing CADA) argue that CADA is a neutral, generally applicable antidiscrimination law regulating commercial conduct in places of public accommodation; applying it to a business selling wedding-website services prevents status-based discrimination and ensures equal access to marketplace goods and services. They contend the law does not compel ideological speech but rather requires offering the same service on equal terms; any speech elements are incidental to regulating discriminatory commercial practices, and prior lower-court precedent (including Masterpiece’s Colorado litigation history) supports enforcement.
key_precedents: Masterpiece Cakeshop, Ltd. v. Colorado Civil Rights Commission, 138 S. Ct. 1719 (2018)
Craig v. Masterpiece Cakeshop, Inc., 370 P.3d 272 (Colo. App. 2015)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the strongest opposing point by analogizing CADA to Rumsfeld v. FAIR—an equal-access rule that may incidentally affect expression—but that analogy breaks down where the regulated "service" is the speaker’s own bespoke, client-specific expressive product. Hurley is closer: a public-accommodations law cannot be applied to force a private speaker to create or incorporate a message she does not wish to convey, and the availability of a disclaimer (as Justice Sotomayor notes) does not cure the injury when the State compels the speech’s creation in the first place. I agree with Justice Kagan’s concern that treating the designer’s customized expression as the public accommodation risks turning antidiscrimination law into a content- and viewpoint-based mandate in expressive markets, triggering strict scrutiny. A narrow, institution-protective holding—limited to genuinely customized, message-bearing speech and leaving CADA fully intact for ordinary goods and nonexpressive services—best addresses Colorado’s interests while avoiding a broader exemption.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on Rumsfeld v. FAIR does not overcome the compelled-speech problem because Colorado is not merely requiring equal access to a forum; it is commanding the petitioner to create custom expressive content celebrating a message she rejects, which Barnette and Wooley forbid as a matter of original public meaning and our compelled-speech precedents. FAIR involved conduct (providing access) that left the schools’ own speech untouched, whereas here the “service” is the speaker’s expression itself—closer to Hurley’s protection against forced inclusion of an unwanted message in a private expressive product. Justice Jackson’s framing of the expressive elements as “incidental” similarly fails under a textualist lens: when the State’s application turns on the content and viewpoint of what must be designed and said, it is direct regulation of speech, not merely commerce. The Communication Clause compounds the constitutional defect by restricting truthful statements about what messages the speaker will or will not create, further confirming viewpoint-based compulsion rather than neutral regulation of sales conduct.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Jackson’s reliance on Rumsfeld v. FAIR is the strongest pushback, but it misdescribes what Colorado is demanding: not equal access to a nonexpressive service, but compelled creation of customized, celebratory speech—closer to Hurley than to FAIR’s regulation of conduct (hosting recruiters) with only incidental speech effects. When the State commands a speaker to produce particular expressive content and forbids her from stating the limits of what she will create, the compulsion is content- and viewpoint-based, triggering the core compelled-speech rule recognized in Barnette and Wooley and reaffirmed in Hurley. The asserted ability to “disavow” cannot cure the constitutional injury where the government is forcing the speaker’s own expressive product into existence, because compelled creation is itself the First Amendment harm. Masterpiece Cakeshop did not decide this question, but it underscores the need for careful, speech-protective limits on CADA when its application reaches expression rather than ordinary commercial conduct.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Chief Justice and Justice Kagan press the hardest point in invoking Hurley: public-accommodations law cannot be used to force a private speaker to incorporate an unwanted message into her own expression. But Colorado’s rule, as applied here, is better understood as an equal-service mandate in the commercial sphere—closer to Rumsfeld v. FAIR—because the State is not scripting celebratory words or requiring ideological affirmation; it is forbidding status-based refusals while leaving the provider free to explain that offering the service does not equal endorsement. Justice Thomas’s Barnette/Wooley framing depends on treating the requested service as inherently a compelled “orthodoxy,” yet the compulsion is to transact on equal terms, not to adopt a government-prescribed viewpoint, and the real-world dignitary and material harms of exclusion in the marketplace weigh heavily in my pragmatic analysis. I agree with Chief Justice Roberts that the Communication Clause raises distinct, more speech-direct concerns and may warrant a narrower as-applied remedy, but that does not justify a broad First Amendment exemption from CADA’s core nondiscrimination requirement.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Jackson’s strongest point is the FAIR analogy: that CADA is a neutral equal-service rule and any speech effect is incidental. But FAIR’s compelled access left the schools’ own speech untouched, while here—just as Chief Justice Roberts stresses—the regulated “service” is the designer’s client-specific expressive product, making the application turn on the content and viewpoint of what must be created, which aligns this case more with Hurley than with FAIR. The availability of a disclaimer does not solve the core First Amendment problem when the State compels the creation of the message in the first instance, and the Communication Clause’s restriction on truthful statements about what the speaker will not create reinforces that Colorado is regulating speech directly rather than merely policing discriminatory conduct. A pragmatic, text-grounded line that preserves CADA for ordinary goods and nonexpressive services while barring compelled bespoke expression remains workable and avoids converting accommodations law into a de facto message mandate.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Jackson’s reliance on Rumsfeld v. FAIR is the strongest counter, but it does not fit these facts: FAIR involved compelled access to recruiters and incidental effects on speech, whereas CADA here commands the creation of bespoke, celebratory expression—content the speaker must author—triggering Barnette/Wooley and Hurley’s bar on using public-accommodations law to force inclusion of unwanted message in a private speaker’s own expression. Even if Colorado characterizes this as regulating “conduct,” the operative command is message-based (what must be designed and what may not be refused), and strict scrutiny applies. Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan correctly note the additional, independent problem of CADA’s Communication Clause: it restricts truthful explanation of the speaker’s expressive limits, reinforcing that the State is regulating speech and viewpoint, not merely commercial transactions. Nothing in the respondents’ framing genuinely undermines the compelled-speech core, so I remain with the petitioner.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson make their best case by analogizing to Rumsfeld v. FAIR and characterizing CADA as an equal-access rule with only incidental effects on speech, but FAIR regulated access/conduct and allowed schools to avoid speaking the government’s message; it did not require the creation of bespoke, client-specific expression. Here, as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan stress, the service being compelled is the speaker’s own customized expressive product, bringing the case closer to Hurley and our compelled-speech line (Barnette/Wooley) than to incidental-burden cases. On an institutional and precedent-based approach, the administrable line is to uphold CADA for ordinary goods and nonexpressive services while forbidding Colorado from compelling the creation of custom expressive content or prohibiting truthful message-based limits under the Communication Clause. That narrower rule answers Justice Jackson’s enforcement-concern by preserving the core of public-accommodations law while maintaining the First Amendment’s traditional protection against government commandeering private expression.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Jackson’s FAIR analogy is the strongest counter, but as Chief Justice Roberts explains, FAIR compelled access and conduct while leaving the schools’ own speech intact; here, the regulated “service” is the creation of bespoke, message-bearing expression, which is direct compulsion under Barnette/Wooley and is closer to Hurley than to incidental speech effects. On a textual and original-public-meaning understanding of the First Amendment, the State cannot require a speaker to author expression celebrating a view she rejects, and the ability to “disavow” does not cure the constitutional injury when the compelled creation is the harm itself. Justice Kagan’s concern about doctrinal administrability reinforces a narrow rule: CADA may reach ordinary sales and standardized services, but not the compelled creation of customized expressive content. The Communication Clause, as Roberts and Justice Thomas note, independently confirms content- and viewpoint-based regulation because it restricts truthful statements about what messages the speaker will and will not create.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan press the best point that bespoke wedding websites are expressive and that Hurley bars using public-accommodations law to force a speaker to include an unwanted message. But that argument depends on recasting CADA’s operative obligation as message-compulsion rather than as equal-service in the commercial marketplace; on my reading, the law targets status-based refusals to deal and leaves substantial room for the seller’s own editorial choices about what to say, making this closer in structure to Rumsfeld v. FAIR’s nondiscriminatory access rule than to Hurley’s forced alteration of an expressive event’s own message. Justice Thomas’s Barnette/Wooley framing highlights that content can matter here, yet it overstates the compulsion where the State is not prescribing any celebratory orthodoxy, only prohibiting categorical exclusion of a protected class from a generally offered service—an application with concrete dignitary and market harms that our doctrine has long allowed States to address. The Communication Clause concerns identified by Roberts, Gorsuch, and Kagan may warrant narrower, as-applied scrutiny of restrictions on truthful explanations, but they do not justify a broad First Amendment carveout that would substantially weaken public-accommodations enforcement for any business that can characterize its service as “expressive.”

John Roberts.reasoning: Colorado’s application of CADA to require a designer to create custom wedding websites celebrating same-sex marriage compels speech in violation of the Free Speech Clause, because the service is inherently expressive and forces the creation of messages the speaker would not otherwise convey. As in Hurley v. Irish-American Gay, Lesbian & Bisexual Group of Boston, a public-accommodations law cannot be applied to mandate inclusion of a message within a private speaker’s own expressive product, even when the law is generally applicable. Masterpiece Cakeshop resolved a narrower Free Exercise issue based on lack of religious neutrality and did not authorize compelled expressive creation, so deciding on compelled-speech grounds here provides a narrow, speech-based rule that preserves the legitimacy of antidiscrimination laws as applied to non-expressive commercial conduct. Any additional restriction under CADA’s “Communication Clause” on announcing the speaker’s service limitations raises an independent content-based speech problem, reinforcing that this enforcement targets expression rather than merely regulating sales conduct.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The First Amendment’s Free Speech Clause, as originally understood, prohibits government from compelling private citizens to speak or to affirm an orthodoxy, and Colorado’s application of CADA here forces an individual engaged in custom, expressive design to create speech celebrating a message she rejects. Barnette holds the State may not “prescribe what shall be orthodox” or force citizens to confess belief “by word or act,” and that principle applies when the State compels expressive output in a private marketplace rather than a public school. Because the compelled creation of a custom wedding website is content- and viewpoint-based compulsion of speech, strict scrutiny applies and Colorado cannot justify compelling this speaker’s expression merely by recharacterizing it as regulation of commercial conduct. The CADA “Communication Clause” likewise burdens protected speech by restricting what she may say about the services she will and will not provide, turning antidiscrimination enforcement into direct regulation of expression.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Applying CADA to require Smith to create custom wedding websites celebrating same-sex marriages compels speech: it forces her to use her expressive talents to convey a celebratory message she does not wish to endorse, which the Free Speech Clause forbids under settled compelled-speech doctrine. As in Hurley v. Irish-American Gay, Lesbian & Bisexual Group of Boston, Colorado may not use a public-accommodations law to mandate inclusion of expressive content or to require a private speaker to alter or host a message as the price of participating in a public-facing expressive enterprise. Colorado’s characterization of this as mere regulation of commercial conduct cannot eliminate the First Amendment problem where the “service” is the creation of customized expression, and CADA’s “Communication Clause” further aggravates the constitutional defect by restricting what the designer may say about the messages she will or will not create. Masterpiece Cakeshop did not resolve the compelled-speech issue on the merits, but its cautions about enforcing CADA in a manner consistent with “neutral and respectful consideration” of First Amendment interests support rejecting an interpretation that effectively mandates viewpoint-conforming expression.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: CADA is a neutral, generally applicable public-accommodations law that regulates commercial conduct—selling services to the public—and its application here requires only equal access to the same wedding-website service, not affirmation of any government-prescribed message. Under Rumsfeld v. FAIR, an equal-access requirement that incidentally affects speech does not amount to unconstitutional compelled speech when the provider remains free to disavow the message and the law simply bars discriminatory refusals of service. Unlike Hurley or Dale, this is not an expressive association being forced to adopt or broadcast an ideological viewpoint; it is a business choosing to operate in the public marketplace and thus obliged to serve customers without discrimination. Given the real-world harms of dignitary injury and market exclusion to same-sex couples, Colorado’s interest in ensuring equal access through CADA justifies the incidental speech burden, and any separate “Communication Clause” issue would require a narrower, as-applied analysis rather than a broad exemption from the accommodation mandate.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: As applied here, CADA’s public-accommodations provisions and the related “Communication Clause” would compel a designer engaged in creating custom, client-specific wedding websites to produce and refrain from producing particular celebratory messages, which is a direct regulation of speech rather than merely the sale of a standardized commercial product. Under Hurley v. Irish-American Gay, Lesbian & Bisexual Group of Boston, the State may not use a public-accommodations law to force a speaker to include unwanted expressive content or to treat the speaker’s own expression as the “public accommodation,” because that intrudes on the speaker’s autonomy over message and viewpoint. Colorado’s interests in equal access are substantial, but a rule that permits compelled creation of tailored celebratory expression is not workable with compelled-speech doctrine and risks turning antidiscrimination law into a tool for viewpoint coercion in expressive services. Masterpiece Cakeshop underscores the constitutional sensitivity of applying CADA in religiously charged contexts, and here the cleaner ground is the Free Speech Clause’s bar on compelled expressive content.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: CADA’s application here compels the creation of custom expressive content celebrating a marriage, and the First Amendment’s compelled-speech doctrine forbids the State from forcing a private speaker to convey a message she does not wish to endorse. As in Barnette and Wooley v. Maynard, the government may not “invade the sphere of intellect and spirit” by requiring affirmation of an objectionable idea, and Hurley confirms that even in a public-accommodations setting the State cannot require a speaker to include or craft expression carrying a message the speaker rejects. Colorado may regulate discriminatory conduct in commerce, but when it commands the production of bespoke speech and also restricts what the speaker may say about her services through CADA’s “Communication Clause,” it crosses a separation-of-powers-and-liberty boundary the First Amendment places beyond state control. Masterpiece Cakeshop did not resolve these merits, but the compelled-speech principles it acknowledged—rooted in the Amendment’s plain protection against “abridging the freedom of speech”—do.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Applying CADA to require Lorie Smith to design bespoke wedding websites celebrating same-sex marriages compels her to create and disseminate an expressive message she would not otherwise convey, triggering the First Amendment’s compelled-speech doctrine rather than mere regulation of commercial conduct. Under Hurley v. Irish-American Gay, Lesbian & Bisexual Group of Boston, a public-accommodations law cannot be used to force a speaker to incorporate and promote a message the speaker does not wish to convey, even when the law is otherwise neutral and generally applicable. Masterpiece Cakeshop left the merits unresolved but confirms that constitutional constraints apply to Colorado’s enforcement mechanisms, and CADA’s “Communication Clause” further raises viewpoint-based speech concerns by restricting what the speaker may say about what messages she will and will not create. Given the need for a workable rule that preserves both anti-discrimination goals and First Amendment protection for compelled expression, Colorado may not compel creation of custom expressive content or bar truthful statements about that expressive limitation.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Applying CADA to require Smith to create custom wedding websites celebrating same-sex marriages compels her to speak a message she would not otherwise convey, implicating the Free Speech Clause’s compelled-speech doctrine. Under Wooley v. Maynard and West Virginia Bd. of Educ. v. Barnette, the First Amendment protects the right to refuse to foster or disseminate an objectionable message, and that protection does not turn on whether the speech is attributed to the speaker. Like the editorial judgments protected in Hurley v. Irish-American Gay, Lesbian & Bisexual Group of Boston and Miami Herald v. Tornillo, Smith’s design choices are expressive and cannot be commandeered merely by labeling the law a regulation of commercial conduct. Colorado may enforce equal-access rules for nonexpressive goods, but CADA’s application here—along with restricting what Smith may say about her services under the Communication Clause—operates as a content- and viewpoint-based compulsion inconsistent with the First Amendment.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: CADA is a neutral, generally applicable public-accommodations law aimed at preventing status-based discrimination in the commercial marketplace, and applying it here regulates the conduct of selling services on equal terms rather than prescribing any government-favored message. Under Rumsfeld v. FAIR, an equal-access requirement that obliges a business to provide the same service to protected-class customers “if, and to the extent,” it provides that service to others imposes at most an incidental burden on speech, unlike the direct message-compulsion found in Hurley and Dale. The State’s compelling interest in ensuring equal access to publicly offered goods and services supports CADA’s application, and any expressive elements in website design are incidental to that nondiscrimination mandate rather than compelled endorsement of same-sex marriage. To the extent the Communication Clause restricts discriminatory advertising, it likewise operates as a regulation of commercial statements tied to unlawful conduct, not viewpoint suppression, consistent with the First Amendment as applied to public-accommodations enforcement.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Colorado may apply its public-accommodations law to compel a web designer to create custom wedding websites celebrating same-sex marriages (and to restrict her speech about that choice) consistent with the First Amendment.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. amend. I (Free Speech Clause and Free Exercise Clause); Colorado Anti-Discrimination Act (CADA) public-accommodations provisions and its related communication provisions (as referenced in the record as the “Communication Clause”).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (303 Creative LLC and Lorie Smith) argue that designing custom wedding websites is inherently expressive activity and that forcing them, under CADA’s public-accommodations and communications restrictions, to create sites celebrating same-sex weddings compels speech and interferes with their ability to speak consistently with their religious beliefs. They contend Colorado is using an antidiscrimination regime to require a creator to convey a state-favored message, and they seek uniform nationwide protection for similarly situated small businesses engaged in custom expressive services.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents (Colorado officials tasked with enforcement) argue that CADA is a neutral, generally applicable public-accommodations law regulating discriminatory commercial conduct, not viewpoint. They maintain that businesses open to the public may not refuse service based on customers’ protected characteristics, and that applying CADA here permissibly ensures equal access to marketplace goods and services. They further dispute that enforcement constitutes unconstitutional compelled speech, emphasizing that the law targets discriminatory refusals, not private beliefs, and that similar challenges have been rejected in other jurisdictions.
key_precedents: Masterpiece Cakeshop, Ltd. v. Colorado Civil Rights Commission, 138 S. Ct. 1719 (2018)
Craig v. Masterpiece Cakeshop, Inc., 370 P.3d 272 (Colo. App. 2015)
Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 550 U.S. 544 (2007)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s FAIR-based framing is the strongest response: that CADA regulates discriminatory commercial conduct and any speech effects are incidental. But FAIR involved compelled access without requiring the regulated party to author customized expression; here, as Justice Kagan stresses, the service is the creation of bespoke, message-bearing content, and CADA (especially coupled with the Communication Clause) operates by compelling and constraining speech in a way Hurley and Wooley/Barnette squarely address. Justice Jackson’s suggestion of disclaimers does not cure the constitutional problem under our compelled-speech cases—once the State forces a speaker to create her own expressive product celebrating a message she rejects, the compulsion is direct, not incidental, and the State’s interest must be pursued by less speech-intrusive means. To preserve institutional legitimacy and avoid a broad carveout, I would keep the holding tightly bound to truly custom expressive services on this record, leaving ordinary public-accommodations enforcement fully intact.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on Rumsfeld v. FAIR is the strongest counter, but it does not fit this case: FAIR upheld an access requirement that did not compel the schools to author or disseminate the government’s message, whereas Colorado here would force the creation of custom, message-laden expression and bar the speaker from stating her policy—classic compelled speech under Barnette and Wooley. As Justice Gorsuch emphasizes, CADA’s application operates in a content- and viewpoint-based way when it requires celebratory speech about a same-sex wedding that the speaker would not otherwise create; that is regulation of speech itself, not merely of commercial conduct. Under the Constitution’s original public meaning, the State lacks authority to commandeer private expression to enforce orthodoxy, even for laudable antidiscrimination objectives. Justice Roberts’s suggestion to limit the holding to genuinely bespoke expressive services is prudent as a matter of judicial restraint, but the First Amendment violation here is categorical once the State compels the speaker’s own words and designs.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s reliance on Rumsfeld v. FAIR identifies the strongest counterpoint—treating CADA as regulating commercial conduct with only incidental expressive effects—but that analogy fails because this service is the creation of custom, message-bearing content, not merely providing equal access to a facility or channel. Here, as Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Colorado’s application (especially coupled with the “Communication Clause”) does not just require serving customers on equal terms; it dictates what the speaker must create and limits what she may say about her reasons, which is classic compelled speech under Barnette, Wooley, and Hurley. Colorado’s antidiscrimination interest is substantial, but it cannot be pursued by commandeering a private citizen’s expressive work product in a way that changes or compels the message. The practical consequence of accepting the State’s position would be a broad power to force speakers in expressive trades to generate speech on contested matters whenever they operate in the public marketplace, which the First Amendment does not permit.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan press Hurley/Barnette/Wooley on the premise that Colorado is compelling “celebratory” bespoke speech, but that framing turns every regulated commercial service with expressive elements into a First Amendment trump over neutral public-accommodations law—precisely the overbreadth Rumsfeld v. FAIR cautions against when equal-access rules are applied without forcing the speaker to adopt the government’s message. Hurley involved an inherently expressive association whose message was altered by compelled inclusion; here the State is regulating a business’s exclusionary conduct in a public marketplace, and attribution/endorsement concerns can be addressed through disclaimers and through an as-applied limitation on the Communication Clause rather than a categorical exemption. Justice Thomas’s reliance on the Communication Clause as “silencing” is a serious point, but it argues for narrowing construction (protect truthful explanations) rather than invalidating CADA’s equal-service requirement itself. Under my pragmatic approach, the real-world impact of carving out “custom speech” from public accommodations is to invite widespread dignitary and material harms to vulnerable groups, without a necessity shown by this record.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Jackson’s FAIR-based point is the hardest: CADA is neutral and generally applicable, and equal-service rules often impose only incidental burdens on speech. But FAIR is meaningfully different because it compelled access without requiring the regulated party to author bespoke, message-bearing content; here, as Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, the record frames the product as customized expressive design, and the Communication Clause further converts an equal-access rule into a speech-compulsion/silencing regime. Hurley and Wooley therefore do more work than FAIR in this posture: Colorado is not just regulating the terms of a sale but directing what expression must be created and limiting how the speaker may explain her policy. To keep the rule workable and coherent with public-accommodations statutes, I would keep the holding narrowly tied to truly custom expressive products, leaving CADA fully enforceable for nonexpressive or off-the-shelf services and for equal-treatment obligations that do not require the vendor’s own words or designs.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is her analogy to Rumsfeld v. FAIR—that CADA regulates commercial conduct and any speech burden is incidental—but that framing does not fit this record because Colorado is not merely requiring equal access to a preexisting, nonexpressive service; it is demanding the creation of bespoke, message-bearing expression and policing what the speaker may say about that choice under the Communication Clause. FAIR involved compelled access and equal treatment without dictating the content of any private party’s speech; here, as Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, the law operates on the content of the product itself and thus triggers Hurley/Barnette/Wooley compelled-speech principles rather than incidental-burden doctrine. Even accepting Colorado’s compelling interest in preventing discrimination, strict scrutiny requires a tighter fit than conscripting this speaker’s own words and designs when the State can secure access through nonexpressive alternatives. Nothing in Justice Jackson’s neutrality-and-marketplace account overcomes the First Amendment’s plain prohibition on compelled affirmation “by word or act,” so my vote remains for the Petitioner.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s and Justice Jackson’s FAIR-based framing is the strongest response, but it still treats as “incidental” what, on this record, is the compelled creation of bespoke, message-bearing celebratory content—closer to Hurley and Wooley/Barnette than to compelled access without authored speech. Chief Justice Roberts is right that the Communication Clause aggravates the constitutional problem by not only compelling the product’s content but also restricting the designer’s ability to explain her policy, making the regime operate in a content- and viewpoint-linked way. Justice Kagan’s limiting principle materially answers institutional and administrability concerns: we can hold narrowly for genuinely custom expressive services while leaving ordinary public-accommodations enforcement fully intact. Under that narrow, precedent-grounded approach, Colorado’s equal-access interest remains compelling but is not pursued through a sufficiently tailored means when it conscripts a speaker’s own expression.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s best point is the FAIR analogy: that CADA regulates commercial conduct and any speech burden is incidental. But FAIR did not require the regulated party to create customized expression at all; it required equal access while leaving schools free to say what they wished, whereas here—on the record as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan stress—the product is bespoke, message-bearing design, and CADA’s application operates on what Smith must create and (via the Communication Clause) what she may say about her policy, bringing the case within Barnette/Wooley/Hurley compelled-speech doctrine rather than incidental-burden doctrine. Justice Jackson’s suggestion that disclaimers can cure attribution does not answer the antecedent problem: the State is still commanding the speaker’s own words and designs in the first instance, and compelled speech is not avoided merely by allowing a later disclaimer. Given that mismatch between means and the State’s concededly compelling end, I remain persuaded this is an as-applied First Amendment violation in the narrow class of truly custom expressive services.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s Hurley/Barnette framing is the most serious challenge, because this record involves customized, message-bearing work and the Communication Clause could, in some applications, chill a vendor’s truthful explanation. But Hurley turned on compelled inclusion that altered the organizer’s own expressive event, whereas CADA here can still be understood—consistent with Justice Sotomayor’s point and Rumsfeld v. FAIR—as an equal-service rule regulating commercial conduct, with any expressive burden incidental so long as Colorado does not attribute the website’s message to the designer as her personal endorsement and allows non-hostile disclaimers. Justice Thomas’s categorical compelled-speech approach presses too far for me because it would constitutionalize a broad carveout from public-accommodations law whenever a business uses expressive tools, without adequate attention to the practical consequences for access to the marketplace and the State’s ability to enforce neutral, generally applicable civil-rights protections. The proper path is an as-applied narrowing that polices the Communication Clause and forbids viewpoint-hostile enforcement, not a First Amendment exemption that disables CADA’s core equal-access function.

John Roberts.reasoning: CADA’s application here, as framed in the record, would require a designer to create customized wedding websites that convey celebratory messages about a same-sex marriage and would also restrict her ability to explain her refusal through the statute’s “Communication Clause,” which together amount to compelled speech in violation of the Free Speech Clause. Under Hurley v. Irish-American Gay, Lesbian & Bisexual Group of Boston, a public-accommodations law may not be used to force a speaker to include or produce expression conveying a message she does not wish to convey, even when the law is generally aimed at preventing discrimination. Consistent with Masterpiece Cakeshop’s emphasis on resolving such disputes on narrow grounds and preserving institutional legitimacy, the ruling should be limited to genuinely custom, expressive services rather than a broad exemption from public-accommodations laws. Colorado remains free to enforce CADA against refusals to sell nonexpressive, off-the-shelf goods or services on equal terms, but it may not compel the creation of speech.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The First Amendment’s text protects the freedom of speech from government compulsion, and Colorado’s application of CADA here would require a speaker to create custom expressive content celebrating a message she rejects, which is compelled speech. Under Barnette, “no official, high or petty” may prescribe orthodoxy in matters of opinion, and Wooley likewise forbids forcing a person to serve as an instrument for disseminating the State’s preferred message. Whatever CADA’s general validity as a public-accommodations statute regulating commercial conduct, its “communication” provisions as applied to a custom website designer operate as content- and viewpoint-based compulsion and restriction of speech, triggering the most exacting scrutiny. Because the Constitution’s original public meaning forbids government from commandeering private expression, Colorado may not enforce CADA to compel the creation of these celebratory websites or to bar the designer from stating her policy.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Applying CADA’s public-accommodations and “Communication Clause” provisions to force Smith to design custom wedding websites celebrating same-sex marriages compels her to create and disseminate speech she would not otherwise express, in violation of the First Amendment. Under Barnette, the State may not prescribe or coerce the affirmation of an ideological message, and Hurley confirms that the government cannot use antidiscrimination law to require an expressive service provider to alter or include speech in a way that changes the message conveyed. Colorado’s asserted interest in ensuring equal access to goods and services, though weighty, cannot justify commandeering a private speaker’s expression when the service is inherently custom and message-based rather than mere nonexpressive commercial conduct. The practical consequence of upholding Colorado’s position would be to give the State broad power to conscript artists and other creators into producing speech endorsing contested views whenever their services are offered to the public.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Colorado’s application of CADA regulates discriminatory commercial conduct in a public marketplace—equal access to goods and services—not the web designer’s private beliefs, and any expressive burden is incidental to a neutral, generally applicable public-accommodations regime. As in Rumsfeld v. FAIR, an equal-access requirement does not become unconstitutional compelled speech merely because complying may require the provider to use the same channels and services for a disfavored group “if, and to the extent,” it offers those services to others. Unlike Hurley or Dale, this is not a case about forcing an expressive association to adopt an ideological message; it is about preventing status-based exclusion from the marketplace, a compelling interest embodied in CADA’s public-accommodations provisions. Masterpiece Cakeshop cautions against religious hostility in enforcement, but it did not create a blanket First Amendment exemption from antidiscrimination laws for businesses open to the public.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: CADA’s public-accommodations and “Communication Clause” provisions, as applied to require Lorie Smith to create custom wedding websites celebrating same-sex marriages, operate as compelled speech because they mandate the content of an expressive product rather than merely regulate nonexpressive commercial conduct under a neutral sales rule. Under Hurley v. Irish-American Gay, Lesbian & Bisexual Group of Boston, the State may not use a public-accommodations law to force a private speaker to include or generate expression conveying a message the speaker does not wish to convey, even when the law’s aim is anti-discrimination. This conclusion can be limited to truly custom, message-bearing design services (workability) and does not license status-based refusals for ordinary, nonexpressive goods; it simply bars Colorado from compelling the creation of celebratory speech or prohibiting Smith from stating her policy. Masterpiece Cakeshop reinforces that these disputes must be resolved consistent with First Amendment constraints when the State’s enforcement intrudes into expressive and religiously motivated decisionmaking.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: CADA’s application here compels a private speaker to create custom expressive content celebrating a message she does not wish to convey, which the First Amendment forbids even when the State pursues laudable policy goals. Under Barnette, the government may not “prescribe what shall be orthodox” or force citizens “by word or act” to affirm a belief, and Colorado’s public-accommodations and “Communication Clause” provisions operate as content-based compulsion when they require the creation of bespoke wedding websites conveying celebratory approval of a same-sex marriage. Unlike a neutral regulation of commercial conduct, this is regulation of expression itself, triggering strict scrutiny, and the State has not shown it must conscript this speaker’s own words and designs—rather than ensure equal access through non-expressive alternatives—to achieve its interests. The separation of powers and the First Amendment’s plain command leave no room for the State to leverage antidiscrimination law to mandate speech or silence disfavored speech about the speaker’s own services.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Applying CADA’s public-accommodations and Communication Clause provisions to require a designer to create a custom wedding website celebrating a same-sex marriage compels the creation of speech and triggers strict scrutiny under the compelled-speech doctrine. Under Wooley v. Maynard and West Virginia State Bd. of Educ. v. Barnette, the State generally may not force a private speaker to convey an ideological message she rejects, and Hurley confirms that even antidiscrimination interests cannot be pursued by compelling expressive content in a way that alters the speaker’s message. Colorado remains free to enforce CADA against status-based refusals of nonexpressive goods and services, but as applied to bespoke expressive websites the law is not a workable fit with the First Amendment because it commandeers the speaker’s own expression rather than regulating ordinary commercial conduct. Consistent with Masterpiece Cakeshop’s emphasis on constitutional limits in this setting, the First Amendment bars this compelled creation and the attendant restriction on the designer’s ability to explain her choice.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Applying CADA’s public-accommodations and “Communication Clause” provisions to require Smith to design custom wedding websites celebrating same-sex marriages compels her to create and disseminate a message she would not otherwise express, triggering strict scrutiny under the compelled-speech doctrine. As Wooley v. Maynard and West Virginia State Bd. of Educ. v. Barnette teach, the First Amendment forbids the State from making a private speaker an instrument for fostering adherence to an ideological message, and Hurley likewise rejects compelled inclusion of unwanted expressive content in a speaker’s own expression. While Colorado may regulate discriminatory commercial conduct, CADA as applied here operates on the content of Smith’s speech—conditioning her ability to offer custom expressive services on her willingness to produce a state-favored celebratory message. Masterpiece Cakeshop does not resolve this case on Free Exercise grounds alone, but it underscores the constitutional constraints when Colorado’s antidiscrimination enforcement collides with protected expression.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: CADA is a neutral, generally applicable public-accommodations law that regulates commercial conduct—refusals of service based on a protected characteristic—rather than targeting petitioners’ religious beliefs or viewpoint, and applying it here serves the practical, equality-based purpose of ensuring equal access to the marketplace. Unlike Hurley v. Irish-American Gay, Lesbian & Bisexual Group of Boston, where the State compelled a private parade organizer to include an unwanted message in an inherently expressive event, Colorado’s application of CADA can be understood as requiring equal provision of a commercial service without dictating the designer’s personal endorsement, especially where the business holds itself out to the public. Masterpiece Cakeshop counsels careful attention to procedural fairness and governmental neutrality; absent evidence of hostility or uneven enforcement, the State may enforce CADA in a manner that avoids viewpoint discrimination while preventing dignitary and material harms from exclusion. On this record, the balance of practical consequences and equal protection values favors permitting Colorado to enforce its public-accommodations and related communication provisions consistent with the First Amendment.
